strengths: Using label propagation and label spreading within density-ratio Bayesian optimization is a coherent, potentially useful combination, especially when a fixed pool of unevaluated candidates is available. The relationship to BORE, LFBO, and established semi-supervised methods is explained and credited.

The experiments provide promising empirical evidence across synthetic functions, tabular hyperparameter optimization, and NATS-Bench. Comparisons include several classifier implementations of BORE and LFBO alongside GP-based methods, with 20 repeated runs and standard errors. The synthetic and NATS-Bench results show substantial gains in several settings.

The appendices investigate kernel parameters, unlabeled sample counts, sampling distributions, and pool subsampling. Including a comparison without unlabeled data and reporting sensitivity and computational limitations are useful contributions to understanding the method.
weaknesses: The central explanation involving reduced overconfidence and improved exploration is insufficiently established. Section 3.1 defines overconfidence as concentrating high scores in a small region, but does not quantify this property or demonstrate that it predicts optimization failure. Figures 1 and 8 show short Branin trajectories; expanding a high-score region does not itself establish better exploration under an argmax acquisition rule. The optimization results support performance improvements more convincingly than the proposed mechanism.

The experiments do not adequately isolate the contribution of semi-supervised learning from kernel smoothing, bandwidth selection, and randomized selection on acquisition plateaus. Figure 11 includes the relevant comparison without unlabeled data, but fixes beta at 0.5 while the main experiments learn beta; its results are also mixed, with the supervised alternative sometimes performing better. A controlled comparison under the main tuning protocol, together with random-search and matched tie-breaking controls, is needed to establish what produces the gains.

The cluster-assumption justification is unsupported. Sampling truncated Gaussians around evaluated points does not ensure that connected high-density regions share the objective-derived label: such regions can cross the current objective threshold. Appendix C also does not establish that adding unlabeled points necessarily expands the favorable decision region or reduces the stated margin. It appropriately acknowledges that the cited i.i.d. classification results do not directly apply to sequential BO, but those results consequently cannot substantiate the stronger claims made in the main text.

Consequential implementation details remain unspecified, including input scaling and categorical encoding, numerical values for the propagation settings, beta initialization and bounds, and several baseline fitting settings. The stated L-BFGS-B procedure also needs clarification for finite, discrete candidate pools. These choices directly affect graph geometry and comparison fairness. A correctable mathematical inconsistency compounds this ambiguity: the scalar definition of p_ij implies P = W D^{-1}, whereas Section 4.1 states P = D^{-1} W and subsequently uses P transposed in Equation 7.

The breadth and practical efficiency claims need stronger qualification. Continuous optimization is tested only on four two-dimensional functions, leaving the proposed sampling strategy largely untested in higher dimensions. Figure 13 measures sensitivity to subset size with fixed beta, but provides no comparative runtime assessment covering the main algorithm's repeated bandwidth optimization and 1,000 acquisition initializations. Evaluation-count improvements therefore do not establish a computational advantage.

The MNIST experiment provides limited evidence for the stated black-box search challenge. Appendix D.4 constructs embeddings using a classifier trained on 440,000 labeled three-digit images to predict the exact number, achieving 96.9% test accuracy. This supplies substantial objective-relevant supervision. A baseline that ranks candidates using the pretrained classifier's predictions is necessary to establish the added value of BO in this setting; the issue is the benchmark's interpretation, rather than demonstrated train/test leakage.
